content: 1. Burza et al. conducted a randomized, open-label, parallel-arm, phase 3 trial in India to evaluate the efficacy of AmBisome monotherapy and combination therapy with AmBisome and miltefosine for treating visceral leishmaniasis in HIV co-infected patients. The study was published in Clinical Infectious Diseases in February 2022 (PMID: 35147680). 2. Ponte-Sucre et al. highlighted the challenges of drug resistance and treatment failure in leishmaniasis, emphasizing the need for innovative strategies to address these issues in the 21st century. This was published in PLoS Neglected Tropical Diseases in 2017. 3. Ter Horst et al. investigated the outcomes of visceral leishmaniasis and HIV co-infection in Ethiopia, focusing on the impact of antiretroviral therapy and other factors. Their findings were published in Clinical Infectious Diseases in 2008. 4. Cacopardo et al. reported prolonged Th2 cell activation and increased viral replication in HIV-Leishmania co-infected patients despite treatment, as published in Transactions of the Royal Society of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene in 1996. 5. Lopez-Velez et al. compared the use of amphotericin B lipid complex versus no treatment for secondary prophylaxis of visceral leishmaniasis in HIV-infected patients. Their study appeared in Journal of Antimicrobial Chemotherapy in 2004. 6. Villanueva et al. conducted a prospective evaluation and follow-up of European patients with visceral leishmaniasis and HIV-1 co-infection during the era of highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART). This was published in European Journal of Clinical Microbiology & Infectious Diseases in 2000. 7. Castro et al. demonstrated that lymphoproliferative responses to soluble Leishmania antigen (SLA) could predict visceral leishmaniasis relapse in HIV-positive patients. Their findings were published in Acta Tropica in 2016. 8. Botana et al. identified asymptomatic immune responders to Leishmania among HIV-positive patients, as reported in PLoS Neglected Tropical Diseases in 2019. 9. Diro et al. explored the use of pentamidine as secondary prophylaxis to prevent visceral leishmaniasis relapse in HIV-infected patients during the first 12 months of a prospective cohort study. This was published in PLoS Neglected Tropical Diseases in 2015. 10. Diro et al. also examined long-term outcomes and prognostics of visceral leishmaniasis in HIV-infected patients using pentamidine as secondary prophylaxis based on CD4 levels in Ethiopia. Their findings were published in PLoS Neglected Tropical Diseases in 2019. 11. Diro et al. further reported on long-term clinical outcomes in visceral leishmaniasis/HIV co-infected patients during and after pentamidine secondary prophylaxis in Ethiopia. This single-arm clinical trial was published in Clinical Infectious Diseases in 2018. 12. Goswami et al. reviewed the protective efficacy of secondary prophylaxis against visceral leishmaniasis in HIV co-infected patients over the past decade in East India. Their study appeared in American Journal of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene. 13. Gradoni et al. evaluated the activity of liposomal amphotericin B (AmBisome) against Leishmania infantum and its tissue distribution in mice, as published in Journal of Drug Targeting in 1993. 14. The WHO released consolidated guidelines on HIV prevention, testing, treatment, service delivery, and monitoring, emphasizing a public health approach. These guidelines are available on the WHO website. 15. Bhattacharyya et al. proposed IgG1 as a potential biomarker for post-chemotherapeutic relapse in visceral leishmaniasis and its adaptation to a rapid diagnostic test. This was published in PLoS Neglected Tropical Diseases in 2014. 16. Marlais et al. explored the use of IgG1 for rapid monitoring of cure versus relapse in visceral leishmaniasis and its potential for diagnosing post-kala-azar dermal leishmaniasis. Their findings were published in Frontiers in Cellular and Infection Microbiology in 2018. 17. Pagliano et al. presented a case series and systematic review of visceral leishmaniasis in pregnancy, as published in Journal of Antimicrobial Chemotherapy in 2005. 18. Dahal et al. conducted a systematic literature review on visceral leishmaniasis in pregnancy and vertical transmission, highlighting therapeutic challenges. This was published in PLoS Neglected Tropical Diseases in 2021. 19. Badaró et al. reviewed leishmaniasis as a manifestation of immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS) in HIV-infected patients, as published in Journal of the International Association of Providers of AIDS Care in 2015. 20. Cloots et al. identified visceral leishmaniasis-HIV co-infection as a predictor of increased Leishmania transmission at the village level in Bihar, India. This was published in Frontiers in Cellular and Infection Microbiology in 2021. 21. Sunyoto et al. explored community perspectives on barriers to visceral leishmaniasis diagnosis and care in southern Gadarif, Sudan, as published in American Journal of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene. 22. Sunyoto et al. also examined global and country-level barriers to the effective supply of leishmaniasis medicines and diagnostics in East Africa. Their qualitative study was published in BMJ Open. 23. The WHO maintains a model list of essential medicines, which is accessible on their website. 24. Sun Pharma announced FDA approval for generic amphotericin B liposome injection, as detailed in their official release. 25. Balasegaram et al. reviewed the use of liposomal amphotericin B as a treatment for human leishmaniasis, as published in Expert Opinion on Emerging Drugs. 26. The WHO released guidelines for the diagnosis, prevention, and management of cryptococcal disease in HIV-infected individuals, supplementing their 2016 antiretroviral drug guidelines. 27. Dorlo et al. reviewed the pharmacology and therapeutic efficacy of miltefosine in treating leishmaniasis, as published in Journal of Antimicrobial Chemotherapy in 2012. 28. Kip et al. reported low antileishmanial drug exposure in HIV-positive visceral leishmaniasis patients on antiretrovirals in Ethiopia, as published in Journal of Antimicrobial Chemotherapy. 29. Costa et al. investigated the antileishmanial activity of antiretroviral drugs combined with miltefosine, as published in Parasitology Research. 30. The WHO released updated guidelines for the treatment of drug-susceptible tuberculosis and patient care in 2017. 31. De Castro et al. compared standard-dose raltegravir and efavirenz-based antiretroviral treatments for HIV and tuberculosis co-infected patients in a phase 3 trial, as published in The Lancet Infectious Diseases in 2021. 32. Cerrone et al. studied the pharmacokinetics of efavirenz 400 mg once daily co-administered with isoniazid and rifampicin in HIV-infected individuals, as published in Clinical Infectious Diseases in 2019. 33. Hefnawy et al. emphasized the importance of secondary screening with clinical isolates for anti-leishmania drug discovery, as published in Scientific Reports in 2018. 34. The WHO hosted a meeting on neglected tropical diseases and antimicrobial resistance, emphasizing a One Health approach to secure future generations' safety. 35. Alvar et al. reflected on strategies to eliminate visceral leishmaniasis as a public health problem in East Africa, calling for enhanced control measures. This was published in The Lancet Global Health in 2021. 36. Van Griensven et al. highlighted the evidence gap in improving outcomes for tuberculosis in visceral leishmaniasis-HIV co-infected patients, as published in Open Forum Infectious Diseases in 2018.
